Walk in the Spirit
wawk ĭn thē spĭr´ĭt
n. phrase (the believer's ordinary conduct under the Spirit's government; Paul's command in Galatians 5 and its description in Romans 8)
Two Greek verbs lie behind the one English word. Peripateo, to walk about, is the New Testament's usual word for how a man conducts his life; stoicheo, in Galatians 5:25, is to walk in line, to keep step in a rank — a soldier's word.

Biblical Definition

To walk in the Spirit is commanded with a promise attached: “This I say then, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh” (Gal 5:16). The conflict is normal: “the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would” (Gal 5:17). The output is fruit rather than effort: “the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith” (Gal 5:22). The command is repeated with a different verb: “If we live in the Spirit, let us also walk in the Spirit” (Gal 5:25). And Romans makes it the mark of those in whom the law is fulfilled: “who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit” (Rom 8:4).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines walk, figuratively, as to move or go on, to behave, to pursue a particular course of life, and, in Scripture, to live and act or behave; and to walk in the Spirit as to live under the influence and direction of the Holy Spirit.

expand to see more

WALK, v.i. To move slowly on the feet; to step slowly along.

4. To be in motion; to act; to move; to conduct oneself; to pursue a particular course of life.

5. In Scripture, to live and act or behave; to pursue a particular course of life.

To walk in the flesh, to live and act according to the corrupt propensities of the flesh.

To walk in the Spirit, to live and act under the influence and direction of the Holy Spirit.

Key Scripture

Gal 5:16 — "This I say then, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh."

Gal 5:17 — "For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would."

Gal 5:22 — "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith,"

Gal 5:25 — "If we live in the Spirit, let us also walk in the Spirit."

Rom 8:4 — "That the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit."

Modern Corruption

Walking in the Spirit is imagined as an elevated state above the conflict, and Paul describes it as the conflict itself, walked through.

expand to see more

Galatians 5:17 is the verse that dismantles the elevated-state reading, and it is often skipped between the command in 16 and the fruit in 22. The flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh, and these are contrary the one to the other, so that ye cannot do the things that ye would. That is written to people who are walking in the Spirit, as a description of what it is like. The believer who feels the pull of the flesh and is troubled by it is not failing to walk in the Spirit; the trouble is the Spirit's opposition being felt. A man in whom there is no struggle has one party absent.

The two verbs correct two opposite errors. Peripateo in verse 16 is the ordinary word for conduct — how a man walks about, buys, speaks, works, keeps his temper — so the walk is not a devotional exercise but a whole life, and there is no walking in the Spirit that is not visible on Tuesday. Stoicheo in verse 25 is to keep step in line, and it corrects the opposite drift toward a purely private spirituality: the Spirit sets the pace and the direction, and the believer's part is not to lead but to keep rank, which is the humbler and harder thing.

The passage's most important word is fruit, set against the works of the flesh in verse 19. Works are manufactured; fruit grows. A congregation that treats love, joy, peace and the rest as targets to be hit by effort has turned Galatians back into the law Paul wrote it to refute. The command is to walk — to keep going in the Spirit's company and under His direction — and the fruit is what appears on a life so walked, over time, by a process the walker does not control. Romans 8:4 says the righteousness of the law is fulfilled in such people, which is a passive, and deliberately so.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek peripateo (G4043), to walk about, conduct oneself; stoicheo (G4748), to walk in line, keep step; epithumeo (G1937), to lust, desire; karpos (G2590), fruit.

expand to see more

Greek pneumati peripateite (G4043) — walk in the Spirit; Galatians 5:16; the same verb, Romans 8:4, Ephesians 4:1, Colossians 1:10.

Greek pneumati stoichomen (G4748) — let us keep step in the Spirit; Galatians 5:25, 6:16, Romans 4:12, Philippians 3:16.

Greek karpos tou pneumatos (G2590) — the fruit of the Spirit; Galatians 5:22 — singular fruit, nine qualities.

Usage

"“So that ye cannot do the things that ye would” — written to people walking in the Spirit."

"“Let us also walk in the Spirit” — and the second verb means keep step."

"“The fruit of the Spirit” — fruit grows; works are manufactured."
